fuentes/relacion-pigafetta/titulo.texto: Account of the First Voyage Around the World

fuentes/relacion-pigafetta/resumen.texto: Diary of the first circumnavigation of the world, written by one of the survivors of the Magellan and Elcano expedition. It describes the passage through the Río de la Plata and the winter of 1520 in San Julián Bay, where the expedition members met very tall hunters whom they called “patagones,” and it recounts how they captured two of them by deception to take them to Spain.

fuentes/relacion-pigafetta/por_que_impor.texto: It is the first European text on the inhabitants of Patagonia and the origin of its name, which for centuries fed the myth of the Patagonian giants.

fuentes/relacion-pigafetta/leer.0.titulo.texto: The First Voyage Round the World by Magellan (Hakluyt Society, 1874), with Pigafetta’s account translated into English

fuentes/senorio-de-los-incas-cieza/titul.texto: The Lordship of the Incas (second part of the Chronicle of Peru)

fuentes/senorio-de-los-incas-cieza/resum.texto: History of the Incas based on what Cieza heard around 1550 in Cusco from quipucamayocs and Inca nobles. It describes the succession of the Incas, the government of the provinces, the roads, the storehouses and the mitimaes, and recounts the campaigns of Topa Inca toward the Collao and Chile.

fuentes/senorio-de-los-incas-cieza/por_q.texto: It is one of the earliest sources on the Tawantinsuyu, written before the reforms of Viceroy Toledo and the inquiries he ordered to prove that the Incas had been tyrants.

fuentes/senorio-de-los-incas-cieza/leer..texto: Spanish text of the 1880 edition, at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/suma-y-narracion-betanzos/titulo.texto: Summary and Narrative of the Incas

fuentes/suma-y-narracion-betanzos/soport.texto: Manuscript; the first part was published in 1880 and the full text appeared in Palma de Mallorca in 1987

fuentes/suma-y-narracion-betanzos/resume.texto: History of the Incas written at the request of Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, based on what the relatives of the author’s wife, from the panaca of Pachacútec, recounted. It makes Pachacútec the founder of the empire and continues up to the war between Huáscar and Atahualpa.

fuentes/suma-y-narracion-betanzos/por_qu.texto: It is the earliest version from a Cusco noble family, and it shows how each lineage told history in its own favor.

fuentes/suma-y-narracion-betanzos/leer.0.texto: 1880 edition of the first part, at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/informaciones-de-toledo/resumen.texto: Series of interrogations of elderly Indigenous people, curacas and quipucamayocs, carried out by Viceroy Francisco de Toledo between 1570 and 1572 during his general inspection (visita), in Jauja, Cusco and other towns of Peru. The questions aimed to prove that the Incas had conquered the other peoples by force, shortly before the arrival of the Spanish, and that the curacas were not natural lords.

fuentes/informaciones-de-toledo/por_que_.texto: They show how the “tyranny” thesis was built, with chosen witnesses and leading questions, and how it upheld the right of the king of Spain to govern Peru.

fuentes/historia-de-los-incas-sarmiento/.texto: Historia índica (second part of the General History called Índica)

History of the Incas written in Cusco at the request of Viceroy Toledo, based on interrogations of descendants of the royal lineages, and read before them in 1572 for their approval. It holds that the Incas were recent tyrants who subjected the other peoples by force, so the king of Spain could be their legitimate lord. It attributes to Topa Inca the conquest of the Collasuyu, Tucumán and Chile as far as the Maule River.

It is the most detailed chronicle of the Inca conquests, but it was written with a declared political aim: to justify Spanish rule against the criticisms of Las Casas and his followers. At the other extreme, the “Royal Commentaries” of the Inca Garcilaso (1609) presented the Incas as benevolent and civilizing rulers, an image that historians also read as idealized.
English translation by Clements Markham (1907), at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/relacion-de-los-fundamentos-polo.texto: Account of the Grounds for the Notable Harm Caused by Not Respecting the Indians’ Customary Rights

Report for Viceroy Toledo explaining how the Incas distributed land among the Inca, the cult and the communities, how tribute was paid through labor, and how the storehouses worked. It holds that Spanish government should respect those customs so as not to impoverish the Indians.
It is one of the foundations of modern knowledge about the Inca economy, and it shows, within the colonial government itself, a view different from the “tyranny” thesis.

fuentes/gobierno-del-peru-matienzo/sopor.texto: Manuscript, published in Buenos Aires in 1910

fuentes/gobierno-del-peru-matienzo/resum.texto: Treatise on how to govern Peru, written by a judge of the Audiencia of Charcas. It proposes gathering the Indians into towns, organizing their work in the Potosí mines by rotation, limiting the power of the curacas and setting the tribute. It describes the route from Charcas to the Río de la Plata through Tucumán, and justifies Spanish rule with the argument that the Incas had been tyrants.

fuentes/gobierno-del-peru-matienzo/por_q.texto: It was the program Viceroy Toledo applied shortly afterward in the reducciones and the Potosí mita.

fuentes/gobierno-del-peru-matienzo/leer..texto: Buenos Aires edition of 1910, at Internet Archive

fuentes/relacion-de-antiguedades-santa-c.texto: Relación de antigüedades deste reyno del Pirú
Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui

History of the Incas written by a Christian Indigenous man from the south of Cusco, who mixes dynastic tradition with the account of an apostle said to have preached in the Andes before the Spanish. It includes hymns in Quechua and a drawing of the altar of the Coricancha that represents the order of the Andean cosmos.
It is one of the few views of the Incas written by an Andean, and it shows how local elites reinterpreted their past in Christian terms.
Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (1873), with the English translation of the account

fuentes/la-araucana/resumen.texto: Epic poem about the war between Spaniards and Mapuche in Chile, written by a soldier who fought in it between 1557 and 1559. It presents Mapuche leaders such as Caupolicán, Lautaro and Colocolo with the traits of classical heroes and acknowledges the valor of the enemy. Ercilla witnessed the mutilation of the prisoner Galvarino and condemns the execution of Caupolicán, which he did not attend; the trial of the log through which Caupolicán wins command does not appear in the prose chronicles and is considered a literary invention.

fuentes/la-araucana/por_que_importa.texto: It fixed the literary image of the untameable “Araucanian,” which for centuries shaped how Europe, Chile and Argentina viewed the Mapuches.

fuentes/arte-de-la-lengua-de-chile-valdi.texto: Art and General Grammar of the Language Spoken throughout the Kingdom of Chile

The first printed grammar of Mapudungun, with a vocabulary, Christian doctrine and a confessional, written by a Jesuit for the evangelization of the Mapuches. The following year Valdivia published doctrines and vocabularies of the Huarpe languages of Cuyo, the allentiac and the millcayac.
It is the basis for the historical study of Mapudungun and, together with the Huarpe works, almost the only surviving record of those languages.
1887 facsimile reprint of the grammar, vocabulary and confessional, at Internet Archive

fuentes/relacion-de-las-provincias-del-t.texto: Account of the Provinces of Tucumán
Report to the Audiencia of Charcas

Description of the cities and Indigenous towns of the governorship of Tucumán, written by a local resident for the president of the Audiencia of Charcas. It lists the peoples of each valley and plain, such as the Diaguitas, Juríes and Comechingones, along with their languages, crops and ways of life, and it counts the Indians held in encomienda by each city.
It is one of the earliest descriptions of the peoples of the northwest and of Córdoba in the first years of the conquest.
Relaciones geográficas de Indias, vol. II, edition by Jiménez de la Espada (Internet Archive)

fuentes/descripcion-de-la-patagonia-falk.texto: A Description of Patagonia and the Adjoining Parts of South America

Description of the geography and peoples of the pampas and Patagonia, written by an English Jesuit who lived more than thirty years in the Río de la Plata. He distinguishes between the peoples he calls Moluches, Puelches and Tehuelches, describes Cangapol and warns that the Patagonian coast was unprotected against other powers.
It is a central source on the southern peoples in the 18th century. It is often noted that it alarmed the Spanish government and weighed on the founding of the Patagonian settlements of 1779.

fuentes/tratado-de-miraflores/titulo.texto: Treaty of Peace of the Estancia of Miraflores

fuentes/tratado-de-miraflores/autor.texto: Martín Rodríguez and the caciques Ancafilú, Tacumán and Tricnín

fuentes/tratado-de-miraflores/resumen.texto: Treaty signed on March 7, 1820 between Martín Rodríguez, on behalf of the government of Buenos Aires, and the caciques Ancafilú, Tacumán and Tricnín, who also acted for thirteen other chiefs gathered in parley at the Chapaleufú stream. It set as the dividing line the lands already occupied by the landowners, prohibited the inhabitants of Buenos Aires from penetrating further into Indigenous territory, and obliged the caciques to return the livestock they had taken.

fuentes/tratado-de-miraflores/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the treaties written between the Creole government and the peoples of the pampas, and it shows that a “territory of the Indians” was recognized. Martín Rodríguez’s campaigns of 1820–1824 rendered it void.

fuentes/tratado-de-miraflores/leer.0.tit.texto: Text of the treaty on Wikisource

fuentes/viaje-del-beagle/titulo.texto: Diary of a Naturalist’s Voyage Round the World

fuentes/viaje-del-beagle/soporte.texto: Book; first as the third volume of FitzRoy’s “Narrative”

fuentes/viaje-del-beagle/resumen.texto: Diary of the Beagle’s voyage around the world. In 1833 Darwin visited Rosas’s camp on the Colorado River during the campaign against the pampas peoples. He noted what one of the soldiers told him and gave as an “indisputable fact” that female prisoners who appeared to be over twenty were killed in cold blood, and that children were sold or given away as servants. He asked who would believe that such atrocities could be committed in a Christian and civilized country. He also describes the Fuegians of the Beagle Channel in the terms of his time, as “savages” on the lowest rung of humanity.

fuentes/viaje-del-beagle/por_que_importa.texto: It is an outside testimony of Rosas’s 1833 campaign and of the first British contacts with the Yaghans.

fuentes/viaje-del-beagle/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Voyage of the Beagle, at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/narrative-fitzroy/titulo.texto: Narrative of the Surveying Voyages of His Majesty’s Ships Adventure and Beagle

fuentes/narrative-fitzroy/soporte.texto: Book in three volumes and an appendix

fuentes/narrative-fitzroy/resumen.texto: Official account of the British hydrographic surveys of the coasts of Patagonia, Tierra del Fuego and Chile. The first volume is by Phillip Parker King, the second by FitzRoy, and the third is Darwin’s diary. FitzRoy recounts how he took four Fuegians to England in 1830 and returned them in 1833, and he includes vocabularies of Fuegian languages.

fuentes/narrative-fitzroy/por_que_import.texto: It is the main source on the Jemmy Button episode and on the Fuegian peoples before the missions.

fuentes/una-excursion-a-los-indios-ranqu.texto: An Excursion to the Ranquel Indians
Letters published in installments in the newspaper La Tribuna

Account in the form of letters of the journey Mansilla made in March and April 1870, from Fort Sarmiento in southern Córdoba to Leubucó, to negotiate peace with the cacique Mariano Rosas. It describes the life, politics and economy of the Ranqueles, the captives, and the Creoles who had taken refuge among them, and it ironically compares “civilization” and “barbarism.”
It is a direct testimony of an independent Indigenous society a few years before its conquest, and a classic of Argentine literature.

fuentes/at-home-with-the-patagonians/res.texto: Account of the year Musters spent traveling with a Tehuelche band from the Strait of Magellan to Carmen de Patagones, passing through Sayhueque’s País de las Manzanas. It describes the organization of the bands, their seasonal routes, the hunting of guanaco and rhea, and trade with the Chilean and Argentine settlements.

fuentes/at-home-with-the-patagonians/por.texto: It is the most complete description of Tehuelche life before the military campaigns.

fuentes/fronteras-y-territorios-federale.texto: Frontiers and Federal Territories of the Southern Pampas

Book by a frontier commander that analyzes the failure of the system of forts and of rations to allied caciques, which he accuses of feeding the business of suppliers and military chiefs. He proposes moving the frontier to the Río Negro and organizing the conquered lands as federal territories.
It is a critique from within the Army itself of the “frontier business,” and it anticipates the policy of 1878–1884.

fuentes/ley-215-de-fronteras/titulo.texto: Law 215 on the Occupation of the Negro and Neuquén Rivers Line

fuentes/ley-215-de-fronteras/resumen.texto: Law of August 13, 1867 that ordered the army to occupy the north bank of the Neuquén and Negro Rivers, from the cordillera to the sea. It promised the tribes that submitted peacefully “everything necessary for their fixed and peaceful existence,” on lands fixed by agreement subject to approval by Congress, and it ordered a general expedition against those who resisted “until subdued and driven south of the Negro and Neuquén Rivers.”

fuentes/ley-215-de-fronteras/por_que_imp.texto: It is the legal basis invoked by Law 947 of 1878. The Paraguayan War and the lack of funds prevented its enforcement for a decade.

fuentes/ley-215-de-fronteras/leer.0.titu.texto: Text of the law on Wikisource

fuentes/conquista-de-quince-mil-leguas/t.texto: The Conquest of Fifteen Thousand Leagues

fuentes/conquista-de-quince-mil-leguas/s.texto: Book commissioned by the Ministry of War

fuentes/conquista-de-quince-mil-leguas/r.texto: Study commissioned by Julio A. Roca, then Minister of War, to present to Congress the plan to move the frontier to the Río Negro. It gathers the background of the expeditions since colonial times, describes the territory as suitable for ranching and agriculture, and presents the Indigenous peoples as an obstacle to be subdued or dislodged.

fuentes/conquista-de-quince-mil-leguas/p.texto: It was the political foundation of Law 947 and of the 1879 campaign, and it shows how the State framed the “frontier question.”

fuentes/ley-947-de-fronteras/titulo.texto: Law 947 on Frontiers (financing of the campaign to the Río Negro)

fuentes/ley-947-de-fronteras/resumen.texto: Law promulgated on October 5, 1878 that authorized the Executive to spend up to 1,600,000 pesos fuertes to enforce the 1867 law and move the frontier to the Negro and Neuquén Rivers, “after subjugating or dislodging the barbarous Indians of the Pampa.” The spending was covered by a subscription of 4,000 bonds of 400 pesos fuertes, to be paid with lots of the lands to be conquered at one bond per square league, with a maximum of three lots of four leagues per person.

fuentes/ley-947-de-fronteras/por_que_imp.texto: It shows that the 1879 campaign was financed in advance with the lands to be conquered, which passed to the holders of the bonds.

fuentes/ley-947-de-fronteras/leer.0.titu.texto: Text of the law on Wikisource

fuentes/memoria-de-guerra-1879/titulo.texto: Report of the War and Navy Department for 1879

fuentes/memoria-de-guerra-1879/resumen.texto: Annual report of the ministry to Congress. For the operations of 1878 and 1879 it gives five main caciques taken prisoner and one killed (Baigorrita), 1,271 Indigenous “lancers” taken prisoner and 1,313 killed, and 10,513 people of the “chusma” (women, children and elderly) taken prisoner, along with 1,049 “reduced.”

fuentes/memoria-de-guerra-1879/por_que_i.texto: It is the most cited official figure for the campaign, both by those who defend it and by those who call it genocide. It does not count the later deaths of prisoners from hunger and disease.

fuentes/estudio-topografico-olascoaga/ti.texto: Topographic Study of La Pampa and Río Negro

fuentes/estudio-topografico-olascoaga/re.texto: Official report of the 1879 campaign, prepared by the head of the army’s topographic office, with the daily journal, the reports of the divisions and maps of the territory traversed.

fuentes/estudio-topografico-olascoaga/po.texto: It is the official version of the 1879 campaign and the source of many Army data that are still cited.

fuentes/estudio-topografico-olascoaga/le.texto: 1881 edition (Internet Archive, Museo Histórico del Chubut)

fuentes/informe-oficial-comision-cientif.texto: Official Report of the Scientific Commission attached to the General Staff of the Expedition to the Río Negro
Adolfo Doering, Pablo G. Lorentz, Gustavo Niederlein and Federico Schulz
Report of the naturalists who accompanied Roca’s 1879 campaign, covering the geology, flora and fauna of the territory between the Colorado and Negro Rivers.
It shows how science accompanied the military campaign and served to assess lands for sale.

fuentes/viaje-a-la-patagonia-austral/res.texto: Account of Moreno’s journey up the Santa Cruz River to Lake Argentino in 1876–1877, with geographic and archaeological observations and descriptions of the Tehuelches he encountered. It combines scientific interest with the argument that Argentina had to occupy Austral Patagonia ahead of Chile.

fuentes/viaje-a-la-patagonia-austral/por.texto: It was one of the foundations of the Argentine claim to Austral Patagonia, and it shows the role of science in the expansion of the State.

fuentes/viaje-al-pais-de-los-araucanos/t.texto: Journey to the Land of the Araucanians

fuentes/viaje-al-pais-de-los-araucanos/r.texto: Account of Zeballos’s 1879 journey through the central pampas behind the military columns, with geographic data, place names and scenes from the abandoned tolderías. It recounts how he and his companions opened Indigenous graves to take skulls destined for anthropological study.

fuentes/viaje-al-pais-de-los-araucanos/p.texto: It documents the newly conquered territory and the practice of gathering Indigenous remains for museums, the origin of today’s restitution claims.

fuentes/ley-1265-remate-de-tierras/titul.texto: Law 1265 on the Sale of Public Lands at Auction

fuentes/ley-1265-remate-de-tierras/resum.texto: Law of 1882 that ordered the auction sale of lands in the national territories incorporated through the military campaigns.

fuentes/ley-1265-remate-de-tierras/por_q.texto: Together with Law 947 and the military bounty law, it was one of the mechanisms by which conquered land passed into private hands in large holdings.

fuentes/ley-1532-territorios-nacionales/.texto: Law 1532 on the Organization of the National Territories

Law of 1884 that organized the national lands outside the provinces into nine territories: La Pampa, Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego, Misiones, Formosa and Chaco. Each was headed by a governor appointed by the Executive, and its inhabitants did not elect representatives to Congress.
It gave administrative form to the territories conquered in Patagonia and the Chaco, which only became provinces between 1951 and 1990.

fuentes/ley-1628-premios-militares/resum.texto: Law of 1885 that granted land in the conquered territories to the chiefs, officers and soldiers of the Río Negro campaign, in extensions that depended on rank.

fuentes/ley-1628-premios-militares/por_q.texto: Studies of public land show that many soldiers sold their certificates to intermediaries, so those lands also ended up concentrated.

fuentes/campana-del-chaco-victorica/titu.texto: Chaco Campaign: expedition led by the Minister of War and Navy, General Benjamín Victorica

fuentes/campana-del-chaco-victorica/sopo.texto: Official report with dispatches and maps

fuentes/campana-del-chaco-victorica/resu.texto: Official publication with the dispatches, daily journals and maps of the 1884 campaign into the central Chaco, which brought together columns that arrived from Santa Fe, Corrientes, Salta and Formosa on the Bermejo River.

fuentes/campana-del-chaco-victorica/por_.texto: It is the official version of the campaign and of its results, written to present the territory as open to colonization.

fuentes/el-gran-chaco-fontana/resumen.texto: Book of exploration and geography of the Chaco, based on the author’s journeys as an official of the Chaco governorship and on the founding of Formosa. It describes rivers, forests and resources, and the Tobas, Mocoví, Matacos (Wichí) and other peoples, with a view to their subjection and to settling the territory.

fuentes/el-gran-chaco-fontana/por_que_im.texto: It is a firsthand testimony of the State’s advance into the Chaco and of how its protagonists viewed the Chaco peoples.

fuentes/el-gran-chaco-fontana/leer.0.tit.texto: 1977 reprint of the 1881 edition, at Internet Archive

fuentes/viaje-al-pais-de-los-onas/titulo.texto: Journey to the Land of the Onas

fuentes/viaje-al-pais-de-los-onas/resume.texto: Account of the military and scientific expedition that Lista led in 1886–1887 through the north of Tierra del Fuego, with observations on the geography, the selk'nam and their language. The San Sebastián massacre of November 25, 1886, in which soldiers killed nearly thirty selk'nam, was denounced by the expedition’s doctor, Polidoro Segers, and by the Salesians.

fuentes/viaje-al-pais-de-los-onas/por_qu.texto: It is the official version of the first Argentine expedition into the interior of the island, and it should be read together with the denunciations of the massacre.

fuentes/yamana-english-dictionary/soport.texto: Manuscript, published in 1933 by Ferdinand Hestermann and Martin Gusinde

fuentes/yamana-english-dictionary/resume.texto: Dictionary of the Yaghan language with more than 30,000 entries, compiled by Thomas Bridges during his years in Ushuaia and Harberton.

fuentes/yamana-english-dictionary/por_qu.texto: It is the most extensive record of a Fuegian language and the basis of what is known of Yaghan.

fuentes/el-ultimo-confin-de-la-tierra/ti.texto: The Uttermost Part of the Earth

fuentes/el-ultimo-confin-de-la-tierra/re.texto: Memoirs of the Bridges family in Tierra del Fuego, from the Ushuaia mission to the Harberton and Viamonte estancias. It recounts the author’s life among the Selk’nam, whose language he spoke, their ceremonies, and the destruction of that people by disease, paid hunters and the advance of the estancias.

fuentes/el-ultimo-confin-de-la-tierra/po.texto: It is the most cited firsthand testimony on the Selk’nam and the Yaghans in the years of their collapse.

fuentes/die-feuerland-indianer/titulo.texto: The Indians of Tierra del Fuego

fuentes/die-feuerland-indianer/resumen.texto: Ethnographic work on the Selk’nam (1931), the Yaghans (1937) and the Kawésqar (1974), based on the author’s four journeys between 1918 and 1924. It describes social organization, religion and ceremonies, such as the Selk’nam Hain, with photographs taken on site.

fuentes/die-feuerland-indianer/por_que_i.texto: It is the most complete ethnographic record of the Fuegian peoples, made when they were already very few.

fuentes/diario-de-claraz/titulo.texto: Travel Diary of an Exploration to Chubut (1865–1866)

fuentes/diario-de-claraz/resumen.texto: Diary of the journey of the Swiss naturalist from the Negro River to the Chubut, guided by northern Tehuelches, with place names in an Indigenous language, routes, customs and vocabularies.

fuentes/diario-de-claraz/por_que_importa.texto: It is a direct source on the northern Patagonian Tehuelches before the military campaigns.

fuentes/antiquites-de-la-region-andine/t.texto: Antiquities of the Andean Region of the Argentine Republic and the Atacama Desert

fuentes/antiquites-de-la-region-andine/r.texto: Report of the French scientific mission of Créqui-Montfort and Sénéchal de la Grange, in which the Swedish archaeologist Eric Boman, based in Argentina, traveled in 1903 through the puna and the valleys of northwestern Argentina and northern Chile. It describes sites, tombs, objects and the relationship between the archaeological remains and the peoples mentioned in the colonial sources.

fuentes/antiquites-de-la-region-andine/p.texto: It is one of the foundations of the archaeology of northwestern Argentina.

fuentes/antiquites-de-la-region-andine/l.texto: First volume of the 1908 edition, at Internet Archive

fuentes/arte-precolombino-de-la-argentin.texto: Synthesis of the art and material culture of the pre-Hispanic peoples of present-day Argentine territory, organized by the sequence of cultures the author helped define, such as Condorhuasi, Ciénaga, La Aguada, Santa María and Belén.
It fixed the chronology of the northwestern cultures, which is still used as a reference, although several of its categories were later revised.

fuentes/los-inkas-del-kollasuyu/resumen.texto: Archaeological synthesis of the Inca presence in northwestern Argentina and northern Chile, with a survey of roads, tambos, pucarás and administrative centers. It proposes a map and a chronology of the occupation based on the structures recorded in the field.

fuentes/los-inkas-del-kollasuyu/por_que_.texto: For decades it was the reference synthesis on Inca archaeology in Argentina. Later dates corrected part of its chronology.

fuentes/de-quimeras-rebeliones-y-utopias.texto: Of Chimeras, Rebellions and Utopias: The Deeds of the Inca Pedro Bohórquez

Study of the uprising of Pedro Bohórquez and the Calchaquíes, based on colonial court records. It analyzes why a Spanish adventurer could be accepted as an Inca by the valley peoples and by the authorities, and how the Calchaquí resistance ended.
It is the main modern research on the last of the Calchaquí wars.

fuentes/nuestros-paisanos-los-indios/res.texto: General history of the Indigenous peoples of present-day Argentine territory from the conquest to the end of the 20th century, with particular attention to the southern frontier, the Chaco and State policies.

fuentes/nuestros-paisanos-los-indios/por.texto: It was one of the first general syntheses of Argentine history centered on Indigenous peoples and on State policies toward them.

fuentes/los-selknam-chapman/titulo.texto: The Selk’nam: The Life of the Onas

fuentes/los-selknam-chapman/resumen.texto: Anthropological study based on the author’s work with Lola Kiepja and other descendants in the 1960s and 1970s, and on the works of Gusinde and Bridges. It reconstructs Selk’nam society, their ceremonies and the chronology of their destruction at the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th.

fuentes/los-selknam-chapman/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main reference on the Selk’nam, written with testimony from the last people who knew traditional life.

fuentes/memorias-de-expropiacion/titulo.texto: Memories of Dispossession: Subjugation and Indigenous Incorporation in Patagonia (1872–1943)

fuentes/memorias-de-expropiacion/resumen.texto: Research on how the Argentine State subjugated and distributed the Indigenous people of Patagonia after the military campaigns: the prisoner depots, which the author calls concentration camps, the transfers, the distribution of families, the colonies and the loss of land, with official documents and community memories.

fuentes/memorias-de-expropiacion/por_que.texto: It is one of the central works of the current that describes the conquest of Patagonia as a genocidal process.

fuentes/carta-de-barzana-1594/titulo.texto: Letter of Father Alonso de Barzana on the Languages and Nations of Tucumán and Paraguay

fuentes/carta-de-barzana-1594/resumen.texto: Letter written in Asunción by a Jesuit who had done missionary work in Tucumán, listing the Indigenous nations of the governorship and of the Chaco and the languages they spoke, such as Kakán, Tonocoté and Sanavirón, and recounting the work of the first missionaries.

fuentes/carta-de-barzana-1594/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the few direct testimonies on the languages of the northwest before their disappearance.

fuentes/carta-de-barzana-1594/leer.0.tit.texto: Relaciones geográficas de Indias, vol. II, edition by Jiménez de la Espada (Internet Archive)

fuentes/diario-de-luis-de-la-cruz/titulo.texto: Journey from Fort Ballenar to Buenos Aires through Indigenous Lands

fuentes/diario-de-luis-de-la-cruz/soport.texto: Diary, published by Pedro de Angelis in 1835

fuentes/diario-de-luis-de-la-cruz/resume.texto: Diary of the journey that the mayor of Concepción, Luis de la Cruz, made in 1806 from the Chilean frontier to Buenos Aires, crossing the lands of the Pehuenches and Ranqueles with the permission of their caciques. It describes his parleys, his trade, his roads and the rivalries between the groups.

fuentes/diario-de-luis-de-la-cruz/por_qu.texto: It is a firsthand source on the peoples of the cordillera and the central pampas at the beginning of the 19th century.

fuentes/diario-de-luis-de-la-cruz/leer.0.texto: Collection of Pedro de Angelis, vol. I (1836), Internet Archive

fuentes/callvucura-zeballos/soporte.texto: Book, first part of the series “The Piedra Dynasty”

fuentes/callvucura-zeballos/resumen.texto: Account of the life of Calfucurá and of the Salinas Grandes confederation, written a few years after its fall, with documents, letters and testimonies gathered by the author, mixed with novelistic scenes.

fuentes/callvucura-zeballos/por_que_impo.texto: It preserves letters and data on Calfucurá that are not found in other sources, though it was written from the viewpoint of the victorious State.

fuentes/l-homme-americain/soporte.texto: Book, part of his “Voyage dans l’Amérique méridionale”

fuentes/l-homme-americain/resumen.texto: Study of South America’s Indigenous peoples based on the author’s travels between 1826 and 1834. It groups them into “races” and “branches” according to their physical appearance, language and customs, among them the pampas peoples, the Patagonians, the Chiriguanos and the peoples of the Chaco.

fuentes/l-homme-americain/por_que_import.texto: It was one of the first comprehensive classifications of South American peoples. Its racial categories were abandoned, but its descriptions remain a source.

fuentes/exploraciones-en-la-paya/titulo.texto: Archaeological Explorations in the Prehistoric City of La Paya

fuentes/exploraciones-en-la-paya/soporte.texto: Publication of the Facultad de Filosofía y Letras de Buenos Aires

fuentes/exploraciones-en-la-paya/resumen.texto: Report of the excavations at the pre-Hispanic settlement of La Paya, in the Calchaquí Valley (Salta), describing its houses, tombs and objects, among them pieces with Inca influence.

fuentes/exploraciones-en-la-paya/por_que.texto: It is one of the first systematic archaeological works in northwestern Argentina.

fuentes/costumbres-de-los-patagones/sopo.texto: Article, Anales de la Sociedad Científica Argentina, vol. 17, pp. 221–240

fuentes/costumbres-de-los-patagones/resu.texto: Article by Carlos Spegazzini, read at the Sociedad Científica Argentina in May 1884, on the southern Tehuelches (Aonikenk) of the Santa Cruz River coast, whom he saw in January and February and in July 1882. He describes summer and winter tents (toldos), burials under calafate bushes with the dead man's horse sacrificed, and camps furnished almost entirely with European manufactured goods, except for hides, quillangos, bags and saddle gear (recados). He proposes an etymology for “patagones”.

fuentes/costumbres-de-los-patagones/por_.texto: It describes the Tehuelches of Santa Cruz at a time when military campaigns were still under way in northern Patagonia. They were observed by a visitor who stayed only a few weeks, a botanist by training.

personas/topa-inca-yupanqui/resumen.texto: Tenth Inca according to the chronicles, son of Pachacútec. Cieza, Betanzos and Sarmiento de Gamboa credit him with the conquest of the Collasuyu as far as northwestern Argentina, Cuyo and central Chile. The dates of his reign, around 1471–1493, come from the chronology of the chronicler Miguel Cabello Balboa (1586), which the historian John Rowe adopted in 1945, and archaeological dates suggest that the expansion began earlier.

personas/huayna-capac/resumen.texto: Eleventh Inca, son of Topa Inca. According to the chronicles he reinforced the eastern frontier of Collasuyu against the Chiriguanos. He died around 1525–1528 in Quito or in Tomebamba, depending on the chronicle followed, probably from an epidemic that arrived from the coast before the conquistadors; his death opened the war between Huáscar and Atahualpa.

personas/pedro-cieza-de-leon/resumen.texto: Spanish soldier and chronicler who traveled the Andes between 1535 and 1550. The second part of his chronicle, “The Lordship of the Incas,” gathers what quipucamayocs and Inca nobles told him in Cusco about the succession of the Incas and their conquests, including that of the Collao.

personas/juan-de-betanzos/resumen.texto: Spaniard who came to Peru with the conquest, learned Quechua and married Cuxirimay Ocllo (Angelina Yupanqui), widow of Atahualpa and of the panaca of Pachacútec. His “Summary and Narrative of the Incas” (1551) records the version of his wife’s family.

personas/polo-de-ondegardo/resumen.texto: Spanish jurist, corregidor of Potosí and later of Cusco. He investigated how the Incas organized land, tribute and worship, and held that to govern the Indians their earlier customs had to be respected. Viceroy Toledo and the Third Council of Lima used his reports.

personas/juan-de-matienzo/resumen.texto: Spanish jurist, oidor of the Audiencia of Charcas from 1561. In “Government of Peru” (1567) he proposed gathering the Indians into towns and organizing their work in the mines by rotation, and he defended opening a road from Charcas to the Río de la Plata through Tucumán. Viceroy Toledo applied many of his ideas.

personas/francisco-de-toledo/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Peru between 1569 and 1581. He carried out the general inspection (visita) of the viceroyalty, gathered the Indians into reducciones, organized the Potosí mining mita and in 1572 had Túpac Amaru I executed. He commissioned the “Informaciones” and Sarmiento de Gamboa’s history to argue that the Incas had been tyrants and not legitimate lords.

personas/pedro-sarmiento-de-gamboa/resum.texto: Spanish navigator and cosmographer in the service of Viceroy Toledo, for whom he wrote the “Indica History” in 1572, based on interrogations of descendants of the Incas in Cusco. In 1584 he founded the colony of Rey Don Felipe in the Strait of Magellan, whose settlers nearly all died of hunger (Puerto del Hambre).

personas/santa-cruz-pachacuti/nombre.texto: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui

personas/santa-cruz-pachacuti/resumen.texto: Christian Indigenous chronicler of the Canas and Canchis region, south of Cusco, who around 1613 wrote the “Relación de antigüedades deste reyno del Pirú,” with Inca dynastic traditions read in Christian terms and a drawing of the Andean cosmos from the Coricancha temple.

personas/juan-calchaqui/resumen.texto: Cacique of the Calchaquí valleys who, according to Spanish sources, led the uprising of the early 1560s that forced the abandonment of the cities of Londres, Córdoba de Calchaquí and Cañete. Almost everything known about him comes from later Spanish chroniclers, such as Pedro Lozano.

personas/pedro-bohorquez/resumen.texto: Andalusian adventurer who around 1656 had himself recognized as an Inca by the Calchaquíes, while convincing the governor of Tucumán, Alonso de Mercado y Villacorta, that he would serve the Crown. In 1658 he led an uprising, surrendered in 1659 with a promise of pardon, and was executed in Lima in 1667.

personas/alonso-de-mercado-y-villacorta/.texto: Spanish military officer, governor of Tucumán in 1655–1659 and 1664–1670, and of the Río de la Plata between those periods. First he received and recognized Pedro Bohórquez; afterward he led the last Calchaquí campaign and the deportation of the Quilmes and other peoples of the valleys.

personas/tomas-falkner/resumen.texto: English physician and Jesuit who lived in the Río de la Plata from 1731. He did missionary work among the pampas and Tehuelches at the Nuestra Señora del Pilar reduction and knew Cangapol. After the expulsion of the Jesuits he published “A Description of Patagonia” (1774) in England.

personas/cacique-cangapol/resumen.texto: Tehuelche cacique of the Río Negro, whom the Spanish called “the Fierce Cacique,” according to Falkner, who dealt with him and describes him in his work. In the 1740s and 1750s he dominated a wide territory between the Río Negro and the sierras of southern Buenos Aires. His hostility and the clashes between the Buenos Aires militias and the reduced Indigenous peoples led the Jesuits to abandon the Nuestra Señora del Pilar reduction in 1751, and in 1753 he allied himself with the Spanish.

personas/yanquetruz/resumen.texto: Ranquel cacique who led his people in the 1820s and 1830s, based at Leubucó, and confronted the central division of the 1833 campaign. Several Ranquel chiefs bore the name, which makes the dates uncertain.

personas/paine/resumen.texto: Great Ranquel cacique between 1836 and 1844, who brought nearly all the Ranquel groups under his command and waged an intermittent war with Córdoba, San Luis, Santa Fe, Mendoza and Buenos Aires. He was the father of Mariano Rosas.

personas/calfucura/resumen.texto: Mapuche lonco born in Araucanía who crossed into the pampas around 1830 and, after the massacre of the Boroano chiefs at Masallé (1834), dominated a confederation of peoples from Salinas Grandes for almost forty years. He alternated treaties and government rations with malones on the frontier. He was defeated at San Carlos in 1872 and died in 1873.

personas/manuel-namuncura/resumen.texto: Son and successor of Calfucurá at the head of Salinas Grandes. He took part in the great invasion of 1875–1876, resisted the campaigns of 1879–1883 and surrendered at Ñorquín, in Neuquén, in March 1884. The government gave him the rank of colonel and then lands at San Ignacio, on the banks of the Aluminé, where he died.

personas/ceferino-namuncura/resumen.texto: Son of Manuel Namuncurá, born in Chimpay. He studied with the Salesians in Buenos Aires and in Viedma and traveled to Italy to pursue the priesthood, but he died of tuberculosis in Rome in 1905. The Catholic Church beatified him in 2007, and he is the object of popular devotion.

personas/mariano-rosas/resumen.texto: Ranquel cacique, son of Painé. As a child he was captured and taken to an estancia of Juan Manuel de Rosas, who was his godfather at baptism. He escaped and from the late 1850s was the principal Ranquel cacique. In 1870 he received Lucio V. Mansilla at Leubucó and negotiated peace with him.

personas/baigorrita/resumen.texto: Ranquel cacique who took his name from his godfather, the Unitarian colonel Manuel Baigorria, who had taken refuge among the Ranqueles. He was one of the chiefs who dealt with Mansilla in 1870, and he died in 1879, pursued by the troops of the Río Negro campaign.

personas/pincen/resumen.texto: Cacique of the lagoons of western Buenos Aires, one of the last independent chiefs of the Buenos Aires frontier. He was captured by Conrado Villegas’s troops at the end of 1878 and confined on Martín García Island. His birth and death dates are uncertain.

personas/catriel/resumen.texto: Cacique of the pampas people of Azul, of the Catriel dynasty, allies of the Buenos Aires government since Rosas’s time. As a colonel he fought with his lancers alongside the army at San Carlos (1872). In 1874 he joined the Mitrist revolution and, after the defeat, was killed by men of his own tribe, according to accounts of the time.

personas/ignacio-coliqueo/resumen.texto: Boroano Mapuche lonco who, after taking part in the civil wars, settled around 1861 with his people as an ally of the government, in the area of the present-day city of Los Toldos, in Buenos Aires. His community, “the Coliqueo tribe,” kept part of those lands and still exists today.

personas/sayhueque/resumen.texto: Mapuche-Tehuelche lonco of the País de las Manzanas, in southern Neuquén, who for decades maintained agreements with the Argentine government. After the campaigns of 1881–1884 he withdrew to the south and surrendered at Junín de los Andes on January 1, 1885, with several thousand followers.

personas/inacayal/resumen.texto: Tehuelche cacique of northwestern Chubut who had received Francisco Moreno during his journeys. He surrendered at the end of 1884 at Junín de los Andes and was taken prisoner. Moreno obtained that he be taken with his family to the La Plata Museum, where he lived as an informant and object of study until his death in 1888. His remains were returned to Tecka in 1994.

personas/orkeke/resumen.texto: Tehuelche cacique of northern Patagonia who in 1869–1870 guided George Musters on his journey to the País de las Manzanas and Carmen de Patagones. Musters describes him in detail in “At Home with the Patagonians.”

personas/lucio-v-mansilla/resumen.texto: Military officer and writer, nephew of Juan Manuel de Rosas. As commander of the southern Córdoba frontier he traveled in 1870 to the Ranquel tolderías at Leubucó to negotiate peace, and he recounted the journey in “An Excursion to the Ranquel Indians,” published in installments that same year.

personas/alvaro-barros/resumen.texto: Military officer and politician who served as chief of the southern Buenos Aires frontier, interim governor of the province of Buenos Aires (1874–1875) and first governor of Patagonia (1879–1882). In “Frontiers and Federal Territories of the Southern Pampas” (1872) he criticized the system of forts and of rations to allied caciques, and he proposed occupying the Río Negro line.

personas/estanislao-zeballos/resumen.texto: Lawyer, journalist and politician, later foreign minister. In 1878, commissioned by the Minister of War, Julio A. Roca, he wrote “The Conquest of Fifteen Thousand Leagues,” which supported the campaign to the Río Negro. In 1879 he traveled through the pampas behind the troops and gathered Indigenous skulls for anthropological study.

personas/conrado-villegas/resumen.texto: Military officer born in Uruguay who founded Trenque Lauquen (1876), captured Pincén in 1878, and led the 1881–1883 campaigns toward Neuquén and Nahuel Huapi. He died in Paris in 1884.

personas/lorenzo-vintter/resumen.texto: Military officer who in December 1878 received the surrender of Juan José Catriel at Carmen de Patagones, commanded columns in the campaigns to the Andes and, as governor of Patagonia, ordered the final operations against Sayhueque and Inacayal in 1884. He later governed the territories of Río Negro and Formosa.

personas/manuel-jose-olascoaga/resumen.texto: Military officer and surveyor from Mendoza, head of the topographic office of the 1879 campaign, whose “Topographic Study of La Pampa and Río Negro” (1880) is the expedition's official report. He was the first governor of the Neuquén territory and founded Chos Malal.

personas/francisco-p-moreno/resumen.texto: Naturalist and explorer who traveled through Patagonia between 1873 and 1880, founded the Museum of La Plata (1884), and served as Argentina's expert in the boundary dispute with Chile. His museum held the remains of Indigenous people killed in the campaigns and housed prisoners such as Inacayal as objects of study, which underlies the restitution claims made today.

personas/george-musters/resumen.texto: English sailor who in 1869–1870 traveled across Patagonia from south to north, from Punta Arenas to Carmen de Patagones, with a Tehuelche party. He recounted the journey in “At Home with the Patagonians” (1871), the most detailed description of Tehuelche life of his time.

personas/jorge-claraz/resumen.texto: Swiss naturalist who in 1865–1866 traveled through northern Patagonia, from the Negro River to the Chubut, guided by Tehuelches. His diary, published only in 1988, records routes, place names, and customs of the northern Tehuelches.

personas/alcide-dorbigny/resumen.texto: French naturalist who traveled through South America between 1826 and 1834, including Corrientes, northern Patagonia, and Bolivia. In “L'Homme américain” (1839) he proposed one of the first classifications of South American peoples by language and physical appearance.

personas/benjamin-victorica/resumen.texto: Lawyer and military officer, son-in-law of Urquiza, Minister of War and Navy under Derqui and then under Roca (1880–1886). In 1884 he personally led the campaign into the central Chaco, with columns converging on the Bermejo River.

personas/luis-jorge-fontana/resumen.texto: Soldier and naturalist who explored the Chaco and the Pilcomayo, founded Formosa in 1879 and wrote “The Great Chaco” (1881). He was the first governor of the Chubut territory (1884–1894), and in 1885–1886 he led the Chubut Riflemen expedition, with some thirty Welsh settlers, to the 16 de Octubre valley, at the foot of the Andes.

personas/apiaguaiki-tumpa/resumen.texto: Young Chiriguano recognized as “tumpa” (divine envoy) who led the 1891–1892 uprising against the Franciscan missions and the landowners of the Chiriguano mountains, in Bolivia. He was defeated at Kuruyuki and executed; Bolivia declared him a national hero in 2009.

personas/antonio-pigafetta/resumen.texto: Chronicler born in Vicenza who traveled with the Magellan–Elcano expedition (1519–1522) and was one of the few survivors to return to Spain. His account describes the inhabitants of San Julián Bay, whom the expedition called “patagones.”

personas/robert-fitzroy/resumen.texto: British naval officer, commander of the Beagle in its surveys of Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego (1828–1836). In 1830 he took four Fuegians to England, among them Jemmy Button, and returned the survivors in 1833, on the voyage that carried Darwin.

personas/jemmy-button/resumen.texto: Yaghan from the islands of the Beagle Channel, whom FitzRoy took to England in 1830 and returned in 1833. In 1859 he was accused of having instigated the massacre of Anglican missionaries at Wulaia, which he denied; he died in 1864, probably in an epidemic.

personas/allen-gardiner/resumen.texto: British naval officer and missionary who founded the Sociedad Misionera Patagónica, later renamed Sudamericana. His 1850–1851 expedition to Tierra del Fuego ended with the starvation death of the entire group; the society he founded later set up the Ushuaia mission.

personas/thomas-bridges/resumen.texto: Anglican missionary who settled with his family among the Yaghan at Ushuaia in 1871 and compiled a Yaghan–English dictionary of more than 30,000 words. In 1886 he left the mission and founded the Harberton estancia on land granted to him by the Argentine government.

personas/lucas-bridges/resumen.texto: Son of Thomas Bridges, born in Ushuaia, who learned the Yaghan and Selk'nam languages and opened the Viamonte estancia in the north of the island. In “The Uttermost Part of the Earth” (1948) he left a firsthand account of the life of the Selk'nam and of their destruction.

personas/julius-popper/resumen.texto: Romanian engineer who in 1886 led an armed expedition to Tierra del Fuego and mined gold at El Páramo, on San Sebastián Bay, with a militia of his own. Photographs of his expedition show his armed men beside dead Selk'nam, and he is one of those named as responsible for the massacres.

personas/ramon-lista/muerte.lugar.texto: San Ramón de la Nueva Orán

personas/ramon-lista/resumen.texto: Military officer and explorer who in 1886 led the Argentine expedition to Tierra del Fuego, during which his soldiers killed nearly thirty Selk'nam at San Sebastián. He later governed Santa Cruz and, after living among the Tehuelches, wrote in defense of the last of them.

personas/jose-menendez/resumen.texto: Asturian merchant based in Punta Arenas, owner of large sheep estancias on both sides of the Strait of Magellan and in Tierra del Fuego. Historians and Selk'nam descendants name him among the estancieros responsible for the massacres of their people; his defenders maintain that there is no direct evidence that he ordered them.

personas/jose-fagnano/resumen.texto: Italian Salesian priest, apostolic prefect of southern Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego from 1883. He founded the San Rafael mission on Dawson Island (1889) and La Candelaria in Río Grande (1893), to which Kawésqar and Selk'nam were taken; many died there of disease.

personas/martin-gusinde/resumen.texto: German priest and ethnologist who made four trips to Tierra del Fuego between 1918 and 1924, lived among the Selk'nam, Yaghan, and Kawésqar, and photographed their ceremonies, such as the Hain. In 1919 he estimated that only 279 Selk'nam remained.

personas/lola-kiepja/resumen.texto: Selk'nam shaman from the Lake Fagnano area, considered the last person raised in the traditional life of her people. Between 1964 and 1966 the anthropologist Anne Chapman recorded her songs and stories, now a principal source on the Selk'nam language and ceremonies.

personas/cristina-calderon/resumen.texto: Yaghan woman from Puerto Williams, on Navarino Island, the last native speaker of the Yaghan language. She worked with linguists and with her family to record stories and vocabulary of her people.

personas/alonso-de-ercilla/resumen.texto: Spanish soldier and poet who fought in Chile against the Mapuche in 1557–1559. In “La Araucana” (1569–1589) he told that war in verse, with a heroic image of the Mapuche leaders that shaped how they were seen in Europe and America for centuries.

personas/luis-de-valdivia/resumen.texto: Spanish Jesuit who promoted in Chile the “defensive war” (1612–1626), a frontier policy negotiated with the Mapuche. He published in Lima the first grammar of Mapudungun (1606) and doctrines and vocabularies of the Allentiac and Millcayac Huarpe languages (1607).

personas/juan-bautista-ambrosetti/resume.texto: Ethnographer and archaeologist, director of the Ethnographic Museum of the University of Buenos Aires. He studied the ruins of Quilmes in 1897 and from 1908 directed the excavations of the Pucará de Tilcara, among the first systematic archaeological investigations in the Northwest.

personas/alberto-rex-gonzalez/resumen.texto: Archaeologist and one of the pioneers of scientific archaeology in northwestern Argentina: he introduced radiocarbon dating to the country and proposed the sequence of cultures, such as Ciénaga, La Aguada, and Belén. He wrote “Pre-Columbian Art of Argentina” (1977).

personas/anne-chapman/resumen.texto: Franco-American anthropologist who worked with Lola Kiepja and other Selk'nam descendants from 1964 and reconstructed their society, their ceremonies, and the chronology of their destruction in “The Selk'nam: Life of the Onas” (1986).

personas/ana-maria-lorandi/resumen.texto: Anthropologist and historian at the University of Buenos Aires, specializing in colonial Northwest Argentina and Tucumán. Her book “Of Chimeras, Rebellions and Utopias” (1997) studies the uprising of Pedro Bohórquez and the Calchaquíes.

personas/spegazzini/resumen.texto: Italian botanist and mycologist who settled in Argentina. In 1881–1882 he took part in Giacomo Bove's Italian-Argentine expedition to Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego, which put him in contact with the Fuegian peoples and with the Tehuelches of Santa Cruz. He published “Costumbres de los habitantes de la Tierra del Fuego” (1882), “Costumbres de los patagones” (1884), and “Apuntes filológicos sobre las lenguas de la Tierra del Fuego” (Anales de la Sociedad Científica Argentina, 1884), which includes a brief grammar of Yaghan. His Haush vocabulary remained unpublished.

personas/czetz/resumen.texto: Hungarian military officer, general in the army of the 1848 revolution, who arrived in Buenos Aires in 1860 and joined the engineers section of the Argentine Army. Under Sarmiento's presidency he directed the advance of the frontier line against the Indigenous peoples in southern Córdoba, in areas that shortly before had been occupied by Ranquel encampments (tolderías), and he built forts in the area of present-day General Villegas. From 1870 he was the first director of the Colegio Militar de la Nación.

hechos/primeros-pobladores-de-la-patagon.texto: The sites of Piedra Museo and Los Toldos, on the Santa Cruz plateau, have hunter-gatherer occupations dated to about 13,000 years ago, among the oldest in the Southern Cone along with Monte Verde, in Chile. These groups hunted guanacos and also American horses and other animals now extinct. In Chilean Patagonia, Fell’s Cave, near the Strait of Magellan, has “fishtail” points dated to about 11,000 radiocarbon years, excavated by Junius Bird in the 1930s.

hechos/cazadores-de-la-puna/titulo.texto: The Hunters of the Puna and the Beginnings of Herding

hechos/cazadores-de-la-puna/resumen.texto: In caves of the Jujuy puna and the Quebrada de Humahuaca, such as Inca Cueva and Huachichocana, there are hunter-gatherer occupations about 10,000 years old. In the following millennia these groups took up raising llamas, either domesticated locally or adopted from the central Andes, which is debated, and began to cultivate crops: the shift to a life of herders and farmers that gives rise to the valley cultures.

hechos/pinturas-de-la-cueva-de-las-manos.texto: The Paintings of the Cueva de las Manos

The oldest paintings in the canyon of the Pinturas River, in Santa Cruz, date to around 7300 BC, and the site continued to be painted for millennia. They are negative hands, scenes of guanaco hunting, and geometric figures made by hunter-gatherers, distant ancestors of the Patagonian peoples.

hechos/constructores-de-cerritos/titulo.texto: The Builders of the Cerritos of the Littoral

hechos/constructores-de-cerritos/resumen.texto: Starting about 5,000 years ago, groups of hunters, fishers, and horticulturalists in eastern Uruguay, southern Brazil, and the Paraná delta raised earth mounds in flood-prone areas to live on, bury their dead, and hold ceremonies. In the delta and the middle Paraná, pottery with animal figures of the so-called Goya-Malabrigo tradition is associated with the ancestors of the Chaná and Timbú.

hechos/cultura-tafi/resumen.texto: Farming peoples of the Tafí valley, in Tucumán, who according to the dates grew maize on terraces, raised llamas, and lived in villages of round stone houses between 300 BC and AD 600. They erected carved monoliths, the menhirs, some with faces in low relief.

hechos/cultura-condorhuasi/resumen.texto: Agricultural and pottery culture of the Hualfín valley, in Catamarca, which according to the usual chronology developed between 400 BC and AD 700. It is known for its modeled pottery, with human and animal figures in complex postures.

hechos/cultura-cienaga/resumen.texto: Culture of farming villages in northwestern Argentina, from the Calchaquí valleys to northern San Juan, centered on the Hualfín valley, which developed in the first centuries of our era. Its cemeteries preserve gray pottery incised with geometric and animal figures.

hechos/cultura-de-la-aguada/resumen.texto: Society of northwestern Argentina that between AD 600 and 900 developed ceremonial centers, such as La Rinconada in the Ambato valley, bronze metallurgy, and an iconography centered on the feline. Its tombs show differences of social rank and a cult shared by several valleys of Catamarca and La Rioja.

hechos/cultura-santamariana/resumen.texto: Culture of the Calchaquí and Yocavil valleys, between 850 and 1480, with large stone settlements such as Quilmes and Tolombón, irrigated crops, and painted funerary urns for burying children. It is the direct antecedent of the Diaguita and Calchaquí peoples whom the Incas and Spaniards met.

hechos/cultura-de-belen/resumen.texto: Culture of the Hualfín and Belén valleys, in Catamarca, defined by Alberto Rex González, which between 1100 and the arrival of the Spaniards built settlements with stone houses and fortresses on hilltops. In its last phase it fell under Inca rule.

hechos/pueblo-omaguaca/resumen.texto: Farming and herding peoples of the Quebrada de Humahuaca, among them the Tilcaras and the Humahuacas, who lived in fortified settlements (pucarás) and came under Inca rule in the 15th century. They resisted the Spaniards until the capture of the cacique Viltipoco in 1594 and were then distributed in encomiendas; their descendants are part of today's Kolla people.

hechos/pueblo-atacama/resumen.texto: Llama herders, oasis farmers and caravan traders of the Atacama puna, in northern Chile and the puna of Jujuy and Salta, who spoke Kunza, a language that became extinct between the late 19th and early 20th centuries. They were incorporated into Tawantinsuyu and later into the colonial system; today they are recognized as Atacameños or Lickanantay on both sides of the mountains. In 1540 Pedro de Valdivia’s force took their pucará of Quitor, next to San Pedro de Atacama.

hechos/pueblo-chicha/resumen.texto: People of the Tupiza region, in southern present-day Bolivia, with a presence in the Jujuy puna, who fell within the Collasuyu. In the colonial period they gave their name to the Chichas corregimiento, and today there are communities that identify as Chicha in Jujuy.

hechos/pueblo-diaguita/resumen.texto: The name the Spanish gave to the farming peoples of the valleys and gorges of Catamarca, La Rioja, Salta, Tucumán, and northern San Juan, and also to those of Chile's Norte Chico, who spoke Kakán, a language now extinct. They grew maize, beans, and squash with irrigation and terraces, raised llamas, and lived in stone settlements; they resisted for more than a century in the Calchaquí Wars and were afterward deported and assigned to encomiendas. Today there are recognized Diaguita communities in Argentina and in Chile.

hechos/pueblo-calchaqui/resumen.texto: Diaguitas of the Calchaquí and Yocavil valleys, divided into parcialidades (subgroups) such as the Pulares, Tolombones, Colalaos, Quilmes, Yocaviles, and Acalianes. They were the core of the resistance to the Spaniards between 1560 and 1667, and after their defeat they were forcibly removed en masse from the valleys.

hechos/pueblo-quilme/resumen.texto: Calchaquí group of the Yocavil valley, in Tucumán, whose fortified settlement is today the Sacred City of Quilmes; they spoke Kakán, which Quechua began to replace from the 15th century. They were among the last to surrender, in 1665. The authorities ordered about two thousand moved to Buenos Aires, where about two hundred families arrived, and there the reducción that gave rise to the city of Quilmes was founded for them. Today their descendants claim and manage the original site.

hechos/pueblo-capayan/resumen.texto: Farming people of western La Rioja and northern San Juan whom the Spanish distinguished from the neighboring Diaguitas by their language. They were assigned to encomiendas after the founding of La Rioja (1591) and dissolved as a distinct group during the colonial period.

hechos/pueblo-olongasta/resumen.texto: People of the Llanos of La Rioja and nearby areas of San Juan and Córdoba, with an economy based on farming and gathering, especially algarroba. Assigned to encomiendas from the late 16th century, they disappeared as a distinct group during the colonial period.

hechos/pueblo-lule/resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherers of the Tucumán plain and the western edge of the Chaco, whom the first Spaniards encountered in the 16th century. Some groups were gathered into missions by the Jesuits in the 18th century, in Salta and Tucumán, and merged with the rural population.

hechos/pueblo-tonocote/resumen.texto: Farming people of the banks of the Dulce and Salado rivers, in Santiago del Estero, whom the first Spaniards called “juríes,” from the Quechua word for rhea. They were the basis of the first encomiendas of Tucumán and mixed quickly with the colonists; in that same region spread the Santiago Quechua that is still spoken.

hechos/pueblo-comechingon/resumen.texto: People of the sierras of Córdoba and San Luis who lived in semi-subterranean houses, grew maize, beans, and squash, raised llamas, and gathered algarroba, and who spoke two languages or varieties, Henia and Camiare. After the founding of Córdoba in 1573 they were assigned to encomiendas and their population fell; today there are recognized Comechingón communities.

hechos/pueblo-sanaviron/resumen.texto: Farming people of northern Córdoba and southern Santiago del Estero, around the Mar Chiquita lagoon and the Dulce River, who lived in villages protected by palisades. They were assigned to encomiendas from the founding of Córdoba and dissolved as a distinct group during the colonial period.

hechos/pueblo-huarpe/resumen.texto: People of Mendoza, San Juan, and San Luis who grew maize with irrigation, fished and hunted in the Guanacache lagoons, and spoke the Allentiac and Millcayac languages, recorded by Luis de Valdivia in 1607. They came under Inca influence in the 15th century and, after the founding of Mendoza (1561), many were taken to Chile as encomienda laborers; today there are Huarpe communities in Guanacache.

hechos/pueblo-querandi/resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherers of the eastern pampas and the shore of the Río de la Plata, who hunted deer and rheas with bolas. They fought the expedition of Pedro de Mendoza in 1536 and the second Buenos Aires; afterward they were assigned to encomiendas or merged with other pampas peoples, and their language has not survived.

hechos/pueblo-chana/resumen.texto: Fishers, hunters, and horticulturalists of the islands of the Paraná delta and the lower Uruguay River, who moved by canoe. They were settled in villages in Entre Ríos and the Banda Oriental and mixed with the criollo population. Their language was considered extinct until the linguist José Pedro Viegas Barros recorded the version kept by Blas Jaime, of Entre Ríos, considered its last speaker, who died in 2026.

hechos/pueblo-timbu/resumen.texto: Fishing and horticultural people of the Paraná riverbank in central Santa Fe, whom Sebastian Cabot encountered in 1527, near Fort Sancti Spiritus, and later Pedro de Mendoza. They were assigned to encomiendas in Santa Fe and mixed with other peoples and with criollos.

hechos/pueblo-charrua/resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherers and later horsemen of the Banda Oriental and western Entre Ríos, who adopted the horse and feral cattle and fought in the wars of independence and the civil wars. In 1831 the Uruguayan army attacked them at Salsipuedes; today there are Charrúa organizations in Uruguay and Entre Ríos.

hechos/pueblo-minuan/resumen.texto: Mounted people related to the Charrúas, from southern Entre Ríos, the Banda Oriental, and southern Brazil, who traded cattle with the Spanish and Portuguese. At the start of the 19th century they merged with the Charrúas and the rural population.

hechos/guaranies-del-parana/titulo.texto: The Guaraní of the Paraná and the Islands

hechos/guaranies-del-parana/resumen.texto: Guaraní groups that had spread from Paraguay along the Paraná as far as the islands of the delta, where they lived in villages of communal houses and grew maize and manioc. The conquistadors of the 16th century encountered them on the delta islands and along the Paraná coast; in the colonial period they were assigned to encomiendas or gathered into reducciones and merged with the population of the littoral, while farther north the Jesuit reducciones arose.

hechos/pueblo-chiriguano/resumen.texto: Guaraní-speaking people who from the late 15th century settled in the sierras of southeastern Bolivia and northern Salta, where they subdued or assimilated the Chanés. They resisted the Incas, the Spanish, and the Bolivian republic until the defeat at Kuruyuki (1892); from the late 19th century many migrated to work in the sugar mills of Jujuy and Salta, and today they call themselves Ava Guaraní.

hechos/pueblo-chane/resumen.texto: Arawak-speaking farming people of the valleys of southeastern Bolivia and northern Salta, largely subdued by the Chiriguanos, who adopted their agriculture and imposed their Guaraní language on them. Today there are Chané communities in northern Salta.

hechos/pueblo-qom/resumen.texto: Guaycurú-speaking people of the central and eastern Chaco, hunters, fishers, and gatherers, who adopted the horse in the 17th century and resisted Spanish and Argentine incursions. After the campaigns of 1884 and 1911 they were resettled or employed in sugar mills, obrajes, and cotton fields; in 1924 the Napalpí massacre killed hundreds of Qom and Moqoit. Today they are one of the largest Indigenous peoples of Argentina.

hechos/pueblo-mocovi/resumen.texto: Guaycurú people of the southern Chaco and northern Santa Fe, mounted since the 17th century, who for decades attacked the estancias and cities of Santa Fe and Santiago del Estero. The Jesuits founded the San Javier reduction for them (1743); in 1904 a Mocoví uprising in San Javier was suppressed, and today they live in Santa Fe and Chaco.

hechos/pueblo-abipon/resumen.texto: Mounted Guaycurú people of the southern Chaco, between the Bermejo River and northern Santa Fe, hunters and warriors, best known through the work of Dobrizhoffer. The Jesuits settled them at San Jerónimo (1748) and other missions; after the expulsion of 1767 and the wars of the 19th century they dispersed and disappeared as a distinct people.

hechos/pueblo-pilaga/resumen.texto: Guaycurú people of central Formosa, close to the Tobas, hunters, fishers, and gatherers, who came under state control after the campaigns of the early 20th century. In 1947 Gendarmería forces killed hundreds of Pilagás at Rincón Bomba.

hechos/pueblo-wichi/resumen.texto: Mataco-Mataguayo-speaking people of the western Chaco, along the Pilcomayo and Bermejo rivers, fishers, hunters, and gatherers, whom criollos called “matacos.” From the late 19th century many worked seasonally in the sugar mills of Jujuy and Salta; today they are one of the largest Indigenous peoples in the country.

hechos/pueblo-chorote/resumen.texto: Mataco-Mataguayo people of the upper Pilcomayo, on the border between Argentina, Bolivia, and Paraguay, fishers and gatherers. Like the Wichí, from the late 19th century they worked in the northern sugar mills, and today they live in communities in northeastern Salta.

hechos/pueblo-aonikenk/resumen.texto: Nomadic hunters of southern Patagonia, between the Chubut River and the Strait of Magellan, who lived by hunting guanacos and rheas, used hide tents, and adopted the horse in the 18th century; they were the “patagones” Magellan saw in 1520. After estancias occupied their lands they were reduced to small reserves, such as Camusu Aike, and their language is practically extinct.

hechos/pueblo-gununa-kuna/titulo.texto: The Gününa Küna (Northern Tehuelches or Puelches)

hechos/pueblo-gununa-kuna/resumen.texto: Nomadic hunters of northern Patagonia, between the Negro and Chubut rivers, whom Spanish and criollo sources often called “puelches” (people of the east, in Mapudungun), a name also applied to other groups. Many mixed with the Mapuche during the Araucanization, and their language became extinct in the 20th century.

hechos/pueblo-mapuche/resumen.texto: An agricultural and pastoral people of central-southern Chile, speakers of Mapudungun, who resisted the Incas and the Spanish and secured recognition of the Biobío as the frontier in parleys such as that of Quilín (1641). From the 17th century their groups and language spread into the pampas and northern Patagonia; they lost their autonomy in the Argentine (1879–1885) and Chilean (1861–1883) campaigns, and today they are the most numerous Indigenous people in Chile and one of the largest in Argentina. A Real Cédula of 1608 allowed the enslavement of Mapuche captured in war until its abolition (1679, applied in Chile in 1683), and the malocas of both sides took captives.

hechos/pueblo-ranquel/resumen.texto: People of the central pampas, in southern Córdoba, San Luis, and La Pampa, formed in the 18th century by groups of Pehuenche, Mapuche, and pampa origin settled in the caldén woodlands (“ranqueles,” people of the reed beds). They raised and traded livestock, alternated malones and treaties with the criollo governments, and were subdued in 1878–1879; today there are Ranquel communities in La Pampa.

hechos/pueblo-pehuenche/resumen.texto: People of the northern Andes of Neuquén and southern Mendoza, who took their name from the pehuén (araucaria), whose seeds they gathered. They traded salt, livestock, and pine nuts on both sides of the Andes and adopted Mapudungun; in 1816 San Martín negotiated with their caciques the passage of his army at a parliament at Fort San Carlos, in Mendoza.

hechos/pueblo-selknam/resumen.texto: Guanaco hunters of the northern and central Isla Grande of Tierra del Fuego, speaking a Chon language, without canoes or horses, organized into family territories and with initiation ceremonies such as the Hain. Gusinde estimated there were between 3,500 and 4,000 around 1880 and counted 279 in 1919; today their descendants claim their identity.

hechos/pueblo-haush/resumen.texto: Hunters and gatherers of the Mitre Peninsula, at the southeastern tip of Tierra del Fuego, speaking a Chon language related to Selk'nam. They numbered a few hundred in the 19th century and disappeared as a group by the early 20th century.

hechos/pueblo-yagan/resumen.texto: Nomadic canoe people of the southern channels of Tierra del Fuego and Cape Horn, who lived by fishing, shellfish, and sea lions. Without censuses, it is estimated that there were about 3,000 in the mid-19th century; in 1883 the Ushuaia mission held nearly a thousand, and after the epidemics of the 1880s a few hundred remained. The last native speaker of their language, Cristina Calderón, died in 2022.

hechos/pueblo-kawesqar/resumen.texto: Nomadic canoe people of the western channels of Chilean Patagonia, between the Gulf of Penas and the Strait of Magellan. They were taken to the mission on Dawson Island, and some were kidnapped to be exhibited in Europe; today few speakers of their language remain.

hechos/los-collas/titulo.texto: The Collas: From the Kingdom of Titicaca to the Kollas of Jujuy

hechos/los-collas/resumen.texto: In the chronicles, “colla” first designates the Aymara-speaking lordship (and earlier Puquina-speaking) north of Lake Titicaca, with its capital at Hatuncolla, which the Incas conquered in the 15th century. By extension the Incas called Collasuyu, “region of the Collas,” the whole southern quarter of the empire, which reached northwestern Argentina and central Chile; in the colonial period “colla” came to name the people of the highlands. In Argentina the name was adopted in the 20th century by the Andean peoples of Jujuy and Salta (Kollas), who include descendants of Omaguacas, Atacamas, Chichas, and other groups, as well as Quechua speakers.

hechos/conquista-inca-del-noroeste/titul.texto: Inca Conquest of Northwestern Argentina and Cuyo

hechos/conquista-inca-del-noroeste/resum.texto: The chronicles of Cieza, Betanzos, and Sarmiento de Gamboa attribute to Topa Inca, around 1471–1493, the conquest of the Collasuyu as far as Tucumán, Cuyo, and Chile. Radiocarbon dates from sites such as Tilcara, Potrero de Payogasta, and El Shincal suggest that Inca presence in the Northwest began a few decades earlier, around 1400–1450. Inca rule relied on the royal road, on tambos, pucarás, and administrative centers, and on mitimaes brought from other regions; it sought minerals, farmland, and control of the passes to Chile, and subjected peoples paid tribute in labor (mit'a) in the fields, the mines, and the army. Archaeologists debate whether it was a direct occupation of the whole territory or a network of enclaves sustained by alliances with local curacas.

hechos/capacocha-del-llullaillaco/resume.texto: Around 1500 the Incas sacrificed three children on the summit of the Llullaillaco volcano, at 6,739 meters, in a capacocha ceremony that joined religion and political domination over the provinces. The bodies, found in 1999 by Johan Reinhard and Constanza Ceruti, have been displayed since 2007 at the Museum of High-Altitude Archaeology in Salta, a practice some Indigenous communities criticize. Analyses of their hair (Wilson et al., 2013) show that in their last year they consumed more and more coca and alcohol, and the eldest, the so-called Maiden, had a coca quid in her mouth.

hechos/batalla-del-maule/resumen.texto: According to the Inca Garcilaso, an army sent by Topa Inca was stopped at the Maule River by peoples of southern Chile, and that river became the limit of the empire. No early source describes the battle, and many historians doubt that it took place; archaeology places the effective limit of Inca rule in Chile farther north, near the Maipo or Cachapoal rivers.

hechos/resistencia-chiriguana-al-inca/re.texto: In the early 16th century Chiriguano groups attacked the eastern frontier of the Collasuyu and destroyed Inca fortresses, according to Sarmiento de Gamboa and Garcilaso; Huayna Cápac sent armies and reinforced a line of forts, among them Samaipata. The Chiriguanos were never subdued by the Incas.

hechos/encomienda-en-el-tucuman/titulo.texto: Encomienda and Personal Service in Tucumán

hechos/encomienda-en-el-tucuman/resumen.texto: In the governorship of Tucumán, Indigenous people held in encomienda paid tribute mostly with personal labor: weaving cloth in the obrajes, gathering wax and honey, raising livestock, and transport, which the encomenderos justified by the lack of other resources. The ordinances of the oidor Francisco de Alfaro (1612) prohibited personal service and set a fixed tribute, but in practice service continued for much of the 17th century. The fall in the encomended population is attributed to epidemics, forced labor, and relocations.

hechos/guerras-calchaquies/resumen.texto: A series of uprisings by the Diaguita peoples of the Calchaquí, Yocavil, Hualfín, and Famatina valleys against the Spanish of Tucumán, in three major cycles: that of Juan Calchaquí (1560–1563), the great uprising of 1630–1643, and the one that began with Bohórquez (1658–1667). In those years cities such as Londres, Córdoba de Calchaquí, and Cañete were abandoned or destroyed, and the war ended with the defeat of the last peoples in 1665–1667 and their desnaturalización (forced relocation): entire families were moved to encomiendas in Salta, Tucumán, Santiago del Estero, Córdoba, La Rioja, and Buenos Aires.

hechos/alzamiento-de-juan-calchaqui/resu.texto: In the early 1560s the peoples of the Calchaquí valleys, led according to Spanish sources by the cacique Juan Calchaquí, rose against the encomiendas and the cities founded by Juan Pérez de Zurita. The cities of Londres, Córdoba de Calchaquí, and Cañete had to be abandoned, and the valleys remained outside Spanish control for decades.

hechos/gran-alzamiento-diaguita/resumen.texto: In 1630 the peoples of Hualfín, Andalgalá, and the valleys, led by the cacique Chelemín, rose against personal service and attacked Londres and other cities, in the largest uprising of colonial Tucumán. The war lasted until 1643; Chelemín was captured and executed, and many peoples were desnaturalizados and divided among the Spanish settlers.

hechos/alzamiento-de-bohorquez/resumen.texto: In 1657, at Pomán, Governor Alonso de Mercado y Villacorta received with honors Pedro Bohórquez, an Andalusian whom the Calchaquíes recognized as an Inca, and named him their lieutenant in the valleys in the hope that he would reveal mines and pacify the region. In 1658 Bohórquez broke with the Spanish and led an uprising; he surrendered in 1659 with a promise of pardon, was taken to Lima, and executed in 1667, while the war in the valleys continued until 1665.

hechos/desnaturalizacion-de-los-quilmes/.texto: After the last campaign of Governor Mercado y Villacorta, the Quilmes, the last to resist in the Yocavil valley, surrendered in 1665. About two thousand were ordered to be marched on foot to Buenos Aires, but about two hundred families, a little over a thousand people, arrived; for them the reducción of the Exaltación de la Santa Cruz de los Quilmes was founded in 1666. In May 1668, 186 tributaries were counted there, and in 1812 the Primer Triunvirato abolished the reducción. Other peoples of the valleys were distributed in encomiendas in Córdoba, La Rioja, Catamarca, and other cities.

hechos/reducciones-jesuiticas-del-chaco/.texto: From the 1740s the Jesuits founded reducciones on the edge of the Chaco for Mocoví (San Javier, 1743), Abipones (San Jerónimo, 1748, and others), Lules, Vilelas, and Tobas, with support from governments and residents who sought to curb attacks on Santa Fe, Santiago del Estero, and Corrientes. They combined evangelization with livestock raising and agriculture, and after the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767 almost all of them declined or were depopulated.

hechos/alzamiento-de-jujuy-1781/titulo.texto: Uprising of the Tobas and Mestizos of Jujuy

hechos/alzamiento-de-jujuy-1781/resumen.texto: In early 1781, in support of Túpac Amaru's rebellion, Tobas from the San Ignacio reduction on the Jujuy frontier rose under the command of the mestizo José Quiroga, the reduction's interpreter, and threatened the city. The militias of Jujuy and Salta defeated them; the governor of Tucumán, Andrés de Mestre, had the leaders executed and sentenced the other prisoners to forced labor, branded with a hot iron.

hechos/caida-demografica-indigena/titulo.texto: The Decline of the Indigenous Population

hechos/caida-demografica-indigena/resume.texto: Estimates of the Indigenous population of present-day Argentina at the time of contact vary widely depending on the method: Ángel Rosenblat (1954) proposed low figures, on the order of a few hundred thousand people, and the table by Jorge Comadrán Ruiz (1969), completed by INDEC in 1980, gives about 403,000 around 1550, almost half of them in the Northwest; authors of the high-figure school, such as Henry Dobyns, proposed totals for the Americas several times larger. What the encomienda censuses of Tucumán and Córdoba show is a sharp fall in the number of tributaries between the late 16th and late 17th centuries, which contemporary sources attribute to smallpox and measles epidemics, forced labor, wars, and relocations.

hechos/encuentro-de-san-julian/resumen.texto: During the winter stay in San Julián Bay, between March and August 1520, Magellan's expedition had contact with Tehuelche hunters whom it called “patagones.” Pigafetta describes their height, their clothing of guanaco skins, and how the Spanish captured two of them by deceit to take them to Spain.

hechos/batalla-de-curalaba/resumen.texto: On December 23, 1598, Mapuche warriors led by Pelantaro surprised and killed at Curalaba the governor of Chile, Martín García Óñez de Loyola, who had captured Túpac Amaru I in 1572, and nearly all his escort.
