A general uprising followed that destroyed the Spanish cities south of the Biobío River, which remained the frontier for almost three centuries.

hechos/parlamento-de-quilin/resumen.texto: In January 1641 the governor of Chile, the Marquis of Baides, and numerous Mapuche loncos agreed at Quilín to peace and recognized the Biobío River as the frontier, with autonomy for the southern Mapuche in exchange for admitting missionaries and freeing captives. It was the first of a long series of parliaments that regulated the Mapuche frontier during the colonial period.

hechos/araucanizacion-de-las-pampas/resu.texto: Between the 17th and 19th centuries Mapudungun, silverwork, textiles, and Mapuche forms of organization spread from Araucanía to the pampas and northern Patagonia, through the livestock trade, marriages, and the arrival of groups such as the Boroganos (around 1820) and the people of Calfucurá (around 1830). There is agreement about that diffusion but not about how to read it: the version that presented it as an invasion of “Chilean Araucanians” upon “Argentine Tehuelches,” spread from the late 19th century and used to treat the Mapuche as foreigners, is rejected today by a large part of anthropologists and historians, who describe it as a long process of exchange among peoples who moved on both sides of the Andes.

hechos/malones-y-comercio-de-ganado/titu.texto: Malones and Livestock Trade Between the Pampas and Chile

hechos/malones-y-comercio-de-ganado/resu.texto: From the 18th century pampas peoples moved cattle and horses, much of it taken in malones from frontier estancias, along trails such as the “camino de los chilenos” to the Andean passes, to exchange in Chile for silver, textiles, weapons, and liquor. The malones also took captives, above all women and children, and criollo raids on the tolderías did the same; at the same time there was peaceful trade in ponchos, feathers, salt, and hides in frontier towns. The figures of stolen livestock given by criollo governments served to request funds and campaigns and are hard to verify.

hechos/fundacion-del-fuerte-independenci.texto: In April 1823 an expedition led by Governor Martín Rodríguez founded Fort Independencia near the Tandil hills, in lands of Pampas and Tehuelches, after several campaigns that broke the peace of Miraflores. It was the origin of the city of Tandil and of a new line of forts that pushed Indigenous peoples to the south.

hechos/campana-de-rosas-al-desierto/resu.texto: In 1833–1834 Buenos Aires, Mendoza, San Luis, and Córdoba sent three divisions against the peoples of the pampas and northern Patagonia: the Buenos Aires division, led by Juan Manuel de Rosas, reached the Colorado River and Choele Choel, on the Negro River, while the central and right-hand divisions had smaller results and withdrew early. The report published in “El Monitor” in April 1834 gave 1,415 Indigenous dead, 382 prisoners (1,642 with their families), and 409 captives freed, and the final tally issued by the Buenos Aires government raised the figures to 3,200 dead, 1,200 prisoners, and about a thousand captives. Darwin, who visited the camp in 1833, noted, based on what soldiers told him, that female prisoners over twenty were killed. Rosas combined war with pacts with “friendly” caciques; his government and later revisionist historians presented it as the campaign that pacified the frontier, while other authors emphasize its violence and the brevity of the advance.

hechos/negocio-pacifico-de-indios/resume.texto: Rosas's system of delivering periodic rations of cattle, yerba, tobacco, and other goods to “friendly” caciques, such as the Catriel of Tapalqué and Azul, in exchange for peace, information, and auxiliary lancers. It reduced malones on Buenos Aires, although conflicts continued in Córdoba, San Luis, and Santa Fe; after Caseros the system fell apart and the malones grew again.

hechos/matanza-de-masalle/resumen.texto: In September 1834, at Masallé, near Salinas Grandes, Calfucurá and his warriors, who had come from Araucanía, killed the main boroganos caciques, such as Rondeau and Melín, who had recently broken with Rosas. From then on Calfucurá controlled the Salinas Grandes and the cattle routes to Chile.

hechos/batalla-de-sierra-chica/resumen.texto: On May 31, 1855, forces of the State of Buenos Aires under Colonel Bartolomé Mitre were defeated near present-day Olavarría by an alliance of Calfucurá, Juan Catriel, and Cachul. With the defeat at San Jacinto that same year, it halted the advance of the Buenos Aires frontier for a decade.

hechos/excursion-de-mansilla/resumen.texto: Between March and April 1870 Colonel Lucio V. Mansilla, chief of the southern Córdoba frontier, traveled with a small party from Fort Sarmiento to Leubucó to agree on peace with the Ranqueles of Mariano Rosas and Baigorrita. The treaty provided for rations and payments in exchange for peace and the return of captives; its implementation was uneven, and war returned a few years later.

hechos/batalla-de-san-carlos-1872/resume.texto: On March 8, 1872, at Pichi Carhué, near the San Carlos fortín (today Bolívar), the army under General Ignacio Rivas, with lancers of Cipriano Catriel and of the tribe of Coliqueo, defeated the Salinas Grandes confederation of Calfucurá, which had launched a large malón on the frontier. It was the last great battle of Calfucurá, who died the following year.

hechos/invasion-grande-1875/resumen.texto: Between December 1875 and early 1876 thousands of lancers led by Namuncurá, Juan José Catriel, Pincén, and the Ranqueles attacked the Buenos Aires frontier, from Tres Arroyos to Azul and Tandil, while War Minister Adolfo Alsina prepared the advance of the frontier. According to contemporary estimates, they took hundreds of captives and hundreds of thousands of head of cattle, and the government responded by accelerating that advance.

hechos/zanja-de-alsina/resumen.texto: Between 1876 and 1877, by order of War Minister Adolfo Alsina, the army moved the frontier forward to Carhué, Guaminí, Puan, and Trenque Lauquen and dug a ditch with an embankment and forts to halt the malones and the passage of stolen cattle. The advance added about 56,000 square kilometers to the cattle-raising territory; after Alsina's death in 1877, his successor Julio A. Roca abandoned the defensive plan for an offensive to the Negro River.

hechos/campana-al-rio-negro-1879/resumen.texto: From mid-1878, army columns launched surprise attacks on the Pampas toldería encampments, captured caciques such as Pincén and Epumer Rosas, and received the surrender of Juan José Catriel. Between April and June 1879, five divisions, some 6,000 men under War Minister Julio A. Roca, advanced from Buenos Aires, Córdoba, San Luis and Mendoza, and the main column reached Choele Choel, on the Río Negro, on May 25. The 1879 Memoria of the Ministry of War gives for these operations 1,313 Indigenous lancers killed and 1,271 prisoners, plus 10,513 women, children and elderly prisoners. For the governments of the time it was the occupation of the “desert”; researchers such as Walter Delrio, Diana Lenton and Mariano Nagy, and Indigenous organizations, consider it the beginning of a genocidal process, while other historians reject that characterization and describe it as a war of territorial conquest.

hechos/campanas-a-los-andes/titulo.texto: Campaigns to the Andes and Nahuel Huapi

hechos/campanas-a-los-andes/resumen.texto: Between 1881 and 1884, columns led by Conrado Villegas, Lorenzo Vintter and other chiefs occupied Neuquén and the cordillera as far as Nahuel Huapi and Chubut, against the Mapuche and Tehuelche of Namuncurá, Reuquecurá, Sayhueque, Inacayal and others, who in some cases attacked forts. Many groups crossed into Chile, where in those same years the Chilean army was occupying Araucanía.

hechos/combate-de-apeleg/resumen.texto: On February 23, 1883, near the Apeleg stream in western Chubut, army troops fought Tehuelches and Mapuches who were still resisting. It was one of the last combats of the Patagonian campaigns.

hechos/rendicion-de-namuncura/resumen.texto: In March 1884, after years of pursuit, Manuel Namuncurá surrendered at the Ñorquín fort in Neuquén, with about three hundred warriors, through the mediation of the Salesian Domingo Milanesio. The government recognized him with the rank of colonel and years later granted him lands in San Ignacio, on the banks of the Aluminé River.

hechos/rendicion-de-sayhueque/resumen.texto: On January 1, 1885, Valentín Sayhueque, one of the last independent loncos of northern Patagonia, surrendered at Junín de los Andes with thousands of followers, after months of retreat through Chubut. With his surrender and that of Inacayal and Foyel, the military campaigns in Patagonia ended; many of those who surrendered were sent as prisoners to Buenos Aires.

hechos/prisioneros-de-las-campanas/titul.texto: The Prisoners: Martín García and the Distribution of Families

hechos/prisioneros-de-las-campanas/resum.texto: Thousands of prisoners from the 1878–1885 campaigns were taken on foot and by boat to Buenos Aires and confined on Martín García Island and other depots, where many died of smallpox and other diseases. Men were sent to the Army, the Navy, or to work in sugar mills and public works, while women and children were handed over to families as servants, separated from their relatives, as notices and lists published in the newspapers record. The researchers Mariano Nagy and Alexis Papazian, based on some 500 documents, described Martín García as a concentration camp; the term is disputed by other authors, although the transfers and the separation of families are not disputed.

hechos/inacayal-en-el-museo-de-la-plata/.texto: Inacayal and the Prisoners of the La Plata Museum

Francisco Moreno housed Inacayal, Foyel and their families, prisoners of the campaigns, at the La Plata Museum, where they lived as informants and objects of study; several died in the museum, and their bodies went into the collections. In 1994 Inacayal’s remains were returned and buried in Tecka, in Chubut, and since then the museum has returned other remains claimed by Indigenous communities.

hechos/misiones-salesianas-de-la-patagon.texto: The Salesians of John Bosco accompanied the 1879 campaign as chaplains, and in 1880 settled in Carmen de Patagones and Viedma, from where they opened schools, colleges and missions in the conquered territories and baptized many Indigenous people. At times they defended Indigenous people against soldiers and estancieros, but they also concentrated them in missions such as those on Dawson Island and La Candelaria, where many died of disease.

hechos/fueguinos-del-beagle/resumen.texto: In 1830 Robert FitzRoy took four Fuegians to England aboard the Beagle: three Kawésqar and the Yaghan Orundellico, Jemmy Button. One died of smallpox, and the others were educated in England, presented to the monarchs, and returned in 1833, on the voyage carrying Darwin, with the idea of founding a mission. The attempt failed within a few weeks, but the episode awakened the interest of British missionary societies in Tierra del Fuego.

hechos/matanza-de-wulaia/resumen.texto: In November 1859, Yaghans from Wulaia, on Navarino Island, killed eight members of an Anglican mission during a religious service; only the cook survived. Jemmy Button was accused of having instigated the attack, and he denied it in the inquiry held in the Falklands.

hechos/mision-anglicana-de-ushuaia/resum.texto: The South American Missionary Society, heir to Allen Gardiner’s society, established a mission in Ushuaia Bay in 1869, where Thomas Bridges settled with his family in 1871. It attracted hundreds of Yaghans and taught them agriculture and livestock raising, but epidemics, above all the measles outbreak that followed the arrival of the Argentine expedition in 1884, caused massive deaths.

hechos/fundacion-de-ushuaia/resumen.texto: On October 12, 1884, the naval expedition of Augusto Lasserre set up a sub-prefecture next to the Anglican mission at Ushuaia, the first official Argentine settlement in southern Tierra del Fuego. With it came a measles epidemic that killed a large part of the Yaghans at the mission.

hechos/expedicion-de-popper/titulo.texto: Popper’s Expedition to Tierra del Fuego

hechos/expedicion-de-popper/resumen.texto: In 1886 Julio Popper arrived in Tierra del Fuego with an armed expedition, found gold in San Sebastián Bay, and founded the El Páramo gold-washing site, which he defended with a militia of his own and where he even minted coins. A series of photographs of the expedition, which Popper circulated, shows his armed men beside the bodies of selk'nam.

hechos/matanza-de-san-sebastian/resumen.texto: On November 25, 1886, in San Sebastián Bay, soldiers of Ramón Lista’s expedition opened fire on a selk'nam encampment and killed close to thirty people, among them women and children (the sources give 27 or 28 dead). Days later, another encounter left more dead and prisoners. The expedition’s doctor, Polidoro Segers, and the Salesians denounced it, and no one was punished. Since 1992, Tierra del Fuego has commemorated that date as the Día del Indígena Fueguino (Fuegian Indigenous Day).

hechos/genocidio-selknam/titulo.texto: The Destruction of the Selk'nam People

hechos/genocidio-selknam/resumen.texto: Between the 1880s and the 1910s, the selk'nam population fell from some 3,500 to 4,000 people, according to Gusinde’s estimate, to 279 in 1919, according to the same author (Charles W. Furlong had calculated about 800 in 1916). It is documented that gold prospectors such as Popper, the Lista expedition, and employees and hunters hired by large sheep estancias killed selk'nam; that there were payments per dead Indigenous person, according to contemporary testimonies such as those of the Salesians and Lucas Bridges; and that hundreds were deported to the missions on Dawson Island and at Río Grande, where most died of disease. In Punta Arenas, judge Waldo Seguel conducted an inquiry between 1895 and 1904 that blamed only some estancia employees, who were released within a few months. The proportion of deaths from violence versus epidemics, and the personal responsibility of some estancieros, are debated. Since the late 20th century, historians, anthropologists and selk'nam descendants have described it as genocide.

hechos/mision-de-isla-dawson/titulo.texto: San Rafael Mission on Dawson Island

hechos/mision-de-isla-dawson/resumen.texto: In 1889 the Salesian José Fagnano began the San Rafael mission on Dawson Island, under a concession from the Chilean government, to which he took Kawésqar and, from 1895, hundreds of selk'nam captured on the estancias of Tierra del Fuego. The inmates worked at the sawmill and other tasks without pay, and most died of tuberculosis and other diseases. When the mission closed in September 1911, twenty-five selk'nam remained.

hechos/selknam-en-paris-1889/resumen.texto: In 1889 the Belgian merchant Maurice Maître captured eleven selk'nam in Tierra del Fuego and displayed them as “Fuegian cannibals” in Paris, during the Universal Exposition, and afterward in other European cities. Several died before the survivors returned. It is one of the documented cases of the “human zoos” of the late 19th century.

hechos/fundacion-de-formosa/resumen.texto: On April 8, 1879, Luis Jorge Fontana founded Villa Formosa on the Paraguay River, after the arbitral award of U.S. President Hayes (1878) gave Villa Occidental to Paraguay. It became the new seat of the government of the Chaco and the base for the advance against the Qom, Pilagá and Wichí of the interior.

hechos/campana-del-chaco-1884/resumen.texto: Between October and December 1884, War Minister Benjamín Victorica personally led a campaign with columns that advanced from Santa Fe, Corrientes, Salta and Formosa and converged on the Bermejo River, against the Qom, Mocoví and other peoples of the central Chaco. He founded forts and opened the territory to colonization, but Indigenous resistance continued, and the government declared the military occupation of the Chaco over only in 1917.

hechos/trabajo-indigena-en-ingenios/titu.texto: Indigenous Labor in the Sugar Mills and Obrajes

hechos/trabajo-indigena-en-ingenios/resu.texto: From the 1880s, the sugar mills of Jujuy and Salta, such as Ledesma and La Esperanza, took thousands of Wichí, Qom, Chorote, Chiriguano and other Indigenous people from the Chaco each year for the harvest season, through contractors and sometimes with military support. Juan Bialet Massé described their workdays, payment in vouchers, and mortality in 1904. In the Chaco and Santa Fe they were also employed in logging camps and cotton fields, and the State created reductions such as Napalpí (1911) to secure that labor.

hechos/levantamiento-de-san-javier-1904/.texto: In April 1904, Mocoví people of San Javier, in northern Santa Fe, rose up against the settlers who occupied their former lands. Police and armed residents suppressed them and killed several. It is remembered as “the last malón.”

hechos/campana-del-chaco-1911/resumen.texto: In 1911 an army expedition under Colonel Enrique Rostagno traveled through the central Chaco as far as the Pilcomayo and established forts to subdue the last independent Qom, Pilagá and Wichí groups and to secure the border with Bolivia and Paraguay. That same year, the Napalpí reduction was founded in the Chaco to concentrate subjugated Indigenous people.

hechos/batalla-de-kuruyuki/resumen.texto: On January 28, 1892, near Cuevo, in southeastern Bolivia, the Bolivian army, settler militias and allied Chiriguanos defeated the followers of Apiaguaiki Tumpa, who had risen against the Franciscan missions and the landowners. Hundreds of Chiriguanos were killed, followed by executions and the distribution of prisoners. It was the last major armed resistance of the Ava Guaraní.

hechos/matanza-de-salsipuedes/resumen.texto: On April 11, 1831, by the Salsipuedes stream, the Uruguayan army of President Fructuoso Rivera made a surprise attack on the Charrúa, whom he had summoned as allies. According to Rivera’s report, about 40 were killed and some 300 taken prisoner, most of them women and children, later distributed as servants. In 1833 four survivors were taken to Paris and exhibited; the remains of one of them, Vaimaca Perú, returned to Uruguay in 2002.

hechos/indigenas-en-los-censos-de-1869-y.texto: Indigenous People in the Censuses of 1869 and 1895

The first national census (1869) counted 1,737,076 inhabitants and separately added an estimate of 93,138 Indigenous people who lived outside State control in the Chaco, the Pampas and Patagonia, without counting them. The 1895 census added a “calculated Indigenous population” of 30,000 people. Neither census recorded as Indigenous those who lived in towns and estancias, who were counted as part of the general population.

hechos/malon-de-la-paz/resumen.texto: Between May and August 1946, some 170 Kollas from the puna of Jujuy and Salta marched about 2,000 kilometers to Buenos Aires to ask President Perón for the return of their lands, held by large landowners. They were received and housed at the Hotel de Inmigrantes, but then forced to return by train, and their lands were not returned at that time.

hechos/avance-de-la-frontera-al-rio-quin.texto: Advance of the frontier to the Río Quinto

In 1869, with Sarmiento as president and Martín de Gainza as Minister of War, Colonel of Engineers Juan Czetz was put in charge of laying out a new frontier line against the Indigenous peoples. Czetz and Colonel Antonio Benavídez, chief of the southern frontier of Santa Fe, drew up the plans and the forts. Lieutenant Colonel Lucio V. Mansilla, chief of the southern frontier of Córdoba, had the mandate to take the line to the Río Quinto, and from Fort Sarmiento, on that line, he set out in 1870 for Leubucó. The 1869 line was left behind by the advance of the Zanja de Alsina in 1876–1877.

lugares/monte-verde/resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherer campsite near Puerto Montt, in southern Chile, whose main occupation is dated to around 14,500 years before the present. Its acceptance showed that the peopling of the Americas was earlier than the Clovis culture, although some archaeologists still dispute its dates.

lugares/los-toldos/resumen.texto: A group of caves in the Deseado Massif, in northern Santa Cruz, with human occupations almost 13,000 years old according to the dating by Augusto Cardich. Its layers hold stone points, remains of guanaco and extinct fauna, and hand-stencil rock paintings.

lugares/piedra-museo/resumen.texto: Site on the central plateau of Santa Cruz where stone tools were found alongside remains of American horses and other extinct fauna, dated to about 13,000 years before the present, among the oldest in the Southern Cone.

lugares/cueva-de-las-manos/resumen.texto: Cave in the canyon of the Pinturas River, in northwestern Santa Cruz, with negative hand paintings, scenes of guanaco hunting, and geometric figures. The oldest are dated to around 7300 BC. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1999.

lugares/cerritos-de-indios/resumen.texto: More than 3,000 earthen mounds in eastern Uruguay and southern Brazil, built by groups of hunters, fishers and horticulturalists. The oldest, at India Muerta (Rocha), are between 4,200 and 5,000 years old. They served as bases for dwellings, burials and ceremonial spaces in flood-prone areas.

lugares/menhires-de-tafi/resumen.texto: Stone monoliths carved by the Tafí culture about 2,000 years ago in the Tafí Valley, in Tucumán, some with faces in low relief. In the 20th century they were gathered in a park in El Mollar, far from their original location, which makes their study difficult.

lugares/pucara-de-tilcara/resumen.texto: Fortified settlement of the Tilcara, an Omaguaca group, on a hill in the Quebrada de Humahuaca. It was occupied approximately between the 11th and 17th centuries and incorporated into Inca rule in the 15th century. It was excavated from 1908 by Juan B. Ambrosetti and Salvador Debenedetti, and was partly reconstructed in the mid-20th century.

lugares/el-shincal/resumen.texto: Inca administrative and ceremonial center near Londres, in Catamarca, with a large plaza, a ceremonial platform (ushnu) and two terraced hills. It is one of the main Inca sites in the southern Collasuyu and has been a national historic monument since 1997.

lugares/tamberias-del-inca/resumen.texto: Inca administrative center in the Chilecito valley, in La Rioja, at the foot of the Famatina, with residential, ceremonial and storage spaces. It probably controlled the exploitation of the mineral resources of the sierra.

lugares/fuerte-de-samaipata/resumen.texto: A large carved rock and a group of buildings in the eastern hills of Bolivia, a ceremonial center since before the Incas, whom the Incas turned into an enclave on their frontier with the Chiriguanos. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1998.

lugares/qhapaq-nan-argentina/resumen.texto: Argentine stretches of the Inca road network, which entered from the altiplano through the puna and the Quebrada de Humahuaca, and continued along the Calchaquí valleys, Catamarca, La Rioja, San Juan and Mendoza until crossing into Chile. Along the way are tambos, pucarás and centers such as Potrero de Payogasta (Salta), El Shincal (Catamarca), the Tamberías del Inca (La Rioja) and the tambo of Ranchillos (Mendoza). In 2014 UNESCO declared the Qhapaq Ñan a World Heritage Site, with stretches in six countries, among them Argentina.

lugares/ciudad-sagrada-de-quilmes/resume.texto: Remains of the largest pre-Hispanic settlement in Argentina: some one hundred hectares at the foot of the Alto del Rey hill, in the Yocavil valley (Tucumán), with stone dwellings and a fortress. It was the center of the Quilmes until their defeat and deportation in 1665–1666. Partly reconstructed in the 20th century, it is now administered by their descendants.

lugares/reduccion-de-quilmes/nombre.texto: Reducción de la Exaltación de la Santa Cruz de los Quilmes

lugares/reduccion-de-quilmes/resumen.texto: Reduction founded in 1666 south of Buenos Aires for the Quilmes deported from the Yocavil valley. In 1668, 186 Indigenous people paid tribute. The First Triumvirate abolished it in 1812, and its lands gave rise to the city of Quilmes.

lugares/fuerte-independencia/resumen.texto: Fort founded in April 1823 by an expedition of Governor Martín Rodríguez next to the Tandil hills, on lands of the Pampas and Tehuelches, to advance the southern frontier of Buenos Aires. It was the origin of the city of Tandil.

lugares/salinas-grandes-calfucura/resume.texto: Salt flats in eastern present-day La Pampa Province, a source of salt and a meeting point for the cattle trails that led livestock toward Chile. They were the seat of Calfucurá from 1834, and of his son Namuncurá until the army occupied them in 1879.

lugares/leubuco/resumen.texto: A locality in northern present-day La Pampa Province that was the seat of the great Ranquel chiefs, from Painé to Mariano Rosas. Mansilla arrived there in 1870. In 1878 troops occupied it and looted Mariano Rosas’s tomb.

lugares/museo-de-la-plata/resumen.texto: Natural science museum founded in 1884 by Francisco Moreno with his collections and opened in 1888. It gathered thousands of Indigenous human remains, many from people killed in the military campaigns, and in 1886–1888 housed prisoners such as Inacayal. Since the 1990s it has returned remains to the communities that claim them.

lugares/estancia-harberton/resumen.texto: Estancia founded in 1886 by Thomas Bridges on the shore of the Beagle Channel, on land granted by the Argentine government. It is the oldest estancia in Argentine Tierra del Fuego. It remains in the hands of his family and holds collections on the Yaghans.

lugares/mision-la-candelaria/resumen.texto: Mission founded in 1893 by José Fagnano near Río Grande, in Tierra del Fuego, and established in 1897 beside Cape Santo Domingo, where surviving selk'nam from the massacres were taken. Many died there of disease. Today it is a museum and school.

lugares/reduccion-de-napalpi/resumen.texto: State reduction founded in 1911 in the central Chaco to concentrate Qom and Moqoit people and supply labor to obrajes and cotton fields. The massacre of 1924 took place there. Today it is the community of Colonia Aborigen.
